transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-19
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Sara Mitchell (Redwood AE), Tom Lee (Redwood SE), Eve Ramirez (NovaApps Eng Manager), John Park (NovaApps Lead Eng), Rachel Kim (NovaApps Security)

[00:00] Sara Mitchell: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do the usual quick sync on the POC, check integration status, any blockers on SDK function calls or structured outputs, and then next steps. Tom's here to walk through a couple of examples.
[00:18] Eve Ramirez: hi, thanks. quick note we're on a 2 week sprint so timeline's same as before, hoping to validate integration and perf before end of month.
[00:28] Tom Lee: great. John, last week you pushed the SDK wrapper and had some mismatched schema errors when the model returned arrays, is that still happening?
[00:38] John Park: yeah, we still see a handful. sometimes the model returns keys like "user_intent" as string, other times it's nested object, and our parser throws. Couple examples attached in the ticket. transcriber, sorry, the ticket id is tkt-401.
[00:52] Sara Mitchell: ok, that's consistent with a structured-output mismatch. we usually recommend a strict JSON schema and then validate post-response. Tom, want to give quick demo of the SDK function calling pattern?
[01:05] Tom Lee: sure. so the Redwood SDK has a functions parameter, similar to openAI's patterns but with differences. you define a function signature and the model returns a call with arguments. our sample repo shows both synchronous and streaming variants. a couple gotchas: when you enable streaming + function calling you need to buffer partial tool calls and only execute once the function payload is complete, otherwise you'll see truncated json.
[01:35] John Park: that explains some of our truncate errors. we were firing the tool client on the first chunk.
[01:40] Eve Ramirez: how do you recommend dealing with validation? i.e., if the model sometimes swaps types.
[01:48] Tom Lee: recommend two layers: 1) schema enforcement in the prompt (explicit, reduce optional fields), 2) client-side validation using a json schema lib. if mismatch, either run a quick re-call with a targeted prompt to correct, or fall back to a safe default. also consider using the structured-output feature where you provide the expected object shape and Redwood will do light post-processing to coerce types — it's not magic but reduces noise.
[02:12] Rachel Kim: from security perspective, i wanted to double check how tool calls are logged and whether arguments get persisted. our concern is PII in function arguments.
[02:22] Sara Mitchell: good call. by default hosted logs are retained per plan, but for the POC we can enable masking and have you use a private deployment or Dedicated trial so we don't persist sensitive args. we also support KMS for key encryption, and audit logs that record only metadata unless you opt-in to full logging. we'll put the SOC2 + KMS notes in the security pack.
[02:45] Rachel Kim: ok, please send that. also SSO will be needed if we go dedicated.
[02:50] Tom Lee: noted. on the perf side, a couple observations from the 1k sample run you shared: median latency is fine, but tail spikes on long context windows. that's usually KV cache or batching mismatches. are you seeing a lot of varying sequence lengths?
[03:08] John Park: yes, some requests include previous 20 messages so tokens vary 4x to 12x.
[03:14] Tom Lee: alright. two levers: smaller max batch sizes for long-seq requests, and prefix/KV caching for repeated conversation starts. also recommend walking through our batching guide in the SDK: it supports dynamic batching and we expose per-request hints like expected seq length.
[03:33] Eve Ramirez: for streaming, we saw incomplete JSON sometimes — is that the same truncated chunk thing?
[03:38] Tom Lee: yes. streaming returns partial tokens; you need to assemble the full function_call payload. if you use the SDK's stream parser it will emit a "function_complete" event. if you implemented your own stream parser, check buffering strategy.
[03:54] Sara Mitchell: quick recaps: John, you'll run a 2k test and send latency & errors; Tom will set up a dedicated perf run; we'll send SDK examples. anything else on tooling integration?
[04:06] John Park: one more. we plan to call external tools after the model decides on intent — e.g., repo search, billing lookup — and we want to confirm Rust-based microservices can be called reliably.
[04:18] Tom Lee: yes, function calls are language-agnostic; the tool invocation is just a webhook or internal client call. two notes: 1) when calling external services from the runtime, use async retries and idempotency keys; 2) log correlation ids so you can trace across services.
[04:36] Eve Ramirez: any limits on payload sizes for tool args?
[04:40] Tom Lee: 16KB by default in hosted, but Dedicated can be configured higher. for really large blobs we recommend passing references (S3 presigned) to avoid token bloat.
[04:51] Rachel Kim: on the private deployment thread, do you support customer-managed KMS/HSM?
[04:56] Sara Mitchell: yes for Private installs and Dedicated we support customer KMS integration. HSM for on-prem is an add-on. again we'll include specifics in the security pack.
[05:08] John Park: about structured output — sometimes we want arrays of objects with optional fields. the model seems to omit empty arrays. how to force presence?
[05:18] Tom Lee: you can do two things: in the prompt explicitly say "return empty arrays as [] and include all keys", and use a post-processing step that enforces presence. we've added an optional 'shape_enforcement' tool in the SDK that will fill missing keys with empty defaults. it's experimental but helps.
[05:38] Eve Ramirez: can you demo that shape_enforcement?
[05:42] Tom Lee: quick, yes. (Tom walks through code verbally) define expected schema in code, call sdk.parseStructured(response, schema), it returns either a validated object or a list of corrections. in the sample repo there's a node and python example.
[06:05] John Park: we'll try python sample first. our stack is mostly python/flask.
[06:10] Sara Mitchell: noted. we'll share python and a small Rust example for tool invocation.
[06:15] Eve Ramirez: on the model side, are you recommending quantized variants for the POC? we care about latency and cost.
[06:22] Tom Lee: for interactive latency, q4-based quantization often gives best price/perf for Llama-like models. we surfaced a recommended profile in the catalog; for this POC if you want lower cost test runs use the quantized hosted variant, but for peak latency testing we can spin Dedicated with fp16 to see best-case. quantization can slightly affect structured output accuracy, so validate with your eval set.
[06:48] John Park: that tradeoff is fine as long as we can replicate expected outputs.
[06:52] Sara Mitchell: we'll include recommended quantization and model variant notes in the repo README.
[06:57] Rachel Kim: one compliance Q: do you support retention policies per customer, e.g., auto-delete raw transcripts?
[07:05] Sara Mitchell: yes, retention is configurable, and for Dedicated/Private you control retention and retention logs. we'll include the policy doc.
[07:13] Eve Ramirez: on observability, what instrumentation should we add client-side?
[07:18] Tom Lee: instrument token counts, request seq_len, model_variant, latency (p50/p95/p99), and error types. also uniquely tag requests with correlation ids. we can share a Grafana dashboard template.
[07:33] John Park: please do. logs from our run will help you tune batching.
[07:37] Tom Lee: absolutely. also enable KV cache metrics — hit rate is the key. if hit rate low you may be missing prefix matching in prompt structure.
[07:51] Sara Mitchell: any blockers on your side for the week?
[07:54] Eve Ramirez: main blocker is time: John needs to get 2k sample run in. otherwise security wants the docs to sign off before widening test.
[08:04] Rachel Kim: i may need a short call with Tom on the KMS integration details.
[08:08] Tom Lee: happy to do a 30-min dive. i can prep a small diagram showing key rotations and envelope encryption.
[08:16] Sara Mitchell: ok we'll schedule that. final quick recap of next steps and owners.
[08:22] John Park: thanks all. we'll aim for the 2k run by the 26th.
[08:26] Sara Mitchell: thanks everyone, recording this and we'll follow up with the repo link and security pack.
[08:30] Meeting closed.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had some mis-heard terms (e.g., "shape enforcement" was transcribed as "shape and force") and occasional speaker mis-assignments. attached artifacts referenced: github.com/redwood/sdk-examples (private link), security-pack-novaapps.pdf, perf-latency-1k.csv.
